theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What word names the person who guides a group through a meeting or problem-solving process without imposing their own solution?
What one word names a short, regular stand-up team meeting, often at the start of a shift, used to review the day and raise problems?
Six team members each get 3 dots in a multivoting exercise. How many dots can be placed in total?
In a SMART target, what word does the letter "M" stand for?
A team found 12 errors in 4,000 invoices. How many errors is that per 1,000 invoices?
Five weekly figures for order turnaround were 6, 5, 7, 4 and 3 days. What is the mean (average), in days?
What one word names the list of topics for a meeting, with times, sent out before the meeting?
What name is given to a grid that sorts ideas by how much benefit they bring and how hard they are to put in place?
What two-word term names a short, focused improvement project in which a team spends a few days redesigning one process and putting the changes in place?
What two-word term names the written list of agreed tasks, owners and due dates kept from improvement meetings?
What word names the senior manager who supports a team's larger improvement project, provides resources and removes obstacles?
What three-letter abbreviation names the main measures a team uses to track its results, such as calls answered or errors per week?
In one week, 380 of a team's 400 orders were delivered on time. What percentage was on time?
What two-word term names the tendency of some members to put in less effort when work is shared in a group, because others will cover for them?
A team of 8 staff and their leader hold a 15-minute huddle each working day, 5 days a week. How many staff-hours a week does the huddle use, counting all 9 people?

essays.stem: Explain the role of a team leader as a facilitator of continuous improvement, and compare it with a "command and control" approach in which the leader decides every change.
essays.modelAnswer: As a facilitator, the team leader does not supply all the answers. She creates the conditions in which the team finds, tests and applies improvements itself. She links the team's work to the organisation's goals, sets up regular time and simple tools for improvement, runs meetings so that every voice is heard, helps the team use data rather than opinion, coaches members to solve problems, removes obstacles and gets resources from senior managers, and recognises contributions. Under command and control, the leader spots problems, decides the changes and tells staff what to do. This can be quick in a crisis or where safety rules leave no choice. But it uses only one person's knowledge, misses the ideas of the people closest to the work, and often meets resistance because staff do not own the change. Facilitation takes more time at first, but it builds skills, commitment and a habit of improvement that lasts. A good leader facilitates most of the time and directs only when a firm decision is needed quickly.
markingPoints: Describes facilitation: guiding the team to find and apply improvements
Gives at least three facilitation tasks such as meetings, tools, coaching or resources
Describes command and control and where it may suit
Compares the effect on ideas, ownership and resistance
Concludes with a reasoned view on when to use each

essays.stem: Plan how you would set up a system that lets your team of ten at a Kingston insurance office take part in continuous improvement every week.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by explaining to the team why improvement matters, how our work affects customers and the firm's goals, and what part each person will play. We would agree three or four team measures, such as claims processed, average turnaround time and errors, and set SMART targets. A visual board in the office would show these measures, a column for new ideas and the status of each action. A ten-minute huddle at the start of each day would review yesterday's problems, and a forty-minute meeting every Friday would look at the measures, choose ideas to try and review actions. Anyone could add an idea to the board at any time. Ideas would be sorted with an impact-effort grid, and small ideas would be tried within the team straight away. Each action would have an owner and a date in an action log. I would coach members to lead parts of the meetings, recognise contributions at the Friday meeting, report results to my manager monthly and review the system with the team after three months.
markingPoints: Explains the purpose and links to goals
Sets team measures and targets
Sets regular routines: huddle, weekly meeting, visual board
Simple way to raise, choose and track ideas with owners
Coaching, recognition, reporting and review of the system

essays.stem: A call centre team handles 2,000 calls a week. Before an improvement, 70% of calls were resolved on the first contact; afterwards, 82% are. Assume each call not resolved first time leads to one repeat call costing J$250 in staff time. Work out how many fewer repeat calls there are each week and the weekly saving, and explain how you would present the results to the team and to your manager.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the change, 30% of 2,000 calls were not resolved first time, which is 600 repeat calls a week. After the change, 18% are not resolved, which is 360 repeat calls. So there are 600 minus 360, or 240, fewer repeat calls each week. At J$250 each, the saving is 240 times J$250, which is J$60,000 a week. To the team, I would show a run chart of first-contact resolution before and after the change at our weekly meeting, explain what the figures mean for customers who no longer have to call back, and thank the members who came up with and tested the idea by name. I would ask them what has made the difference and what could improve it further. To my manager, I would send a short one-page report giving the problem, the change, the results in calls and money, and the next steps, with a note that the figures should be checked again after three months to make sure the gain holds. I would also suggest sharing the method with other teams.
markingPoints: 600 repeat calls before and 360 after
240 fewer repeat calls a week
Weekly saving of J$60,000
Presents results to the team clearly with recognition and involvement
Reports to the manager concisely with next steps or a check that the gain holds

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and run a one-hour team meeting to choose one improvement to work on, naming the techniques you would use at each stage.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would book a quiet room, send a short agenda with the aim and the latest team data, and prepare a flipchart, sticky notes and dots. I would open by restating the aim and agreeing ground rules, such as one person speaking at a time and no judging ideas during the idea stage, and I would show a parking lot sheet for points off the topic. For ten minutes I would review the data with the team, so that we agree on the biggest problems and write a clear problem statement. Next, members would write ideas silently on sticky notes and then share them in a round-robin, so that quiet members are heard. We would group similar notes into an affinity diagram. Each member would then use three dots to multivote, and we would place the top ideas on an impact-effort grid. The team would agree by consensus on one idea with high impact and low effort. Before closing, we would set a SMART target, record owners and dates in the action log, and agree when we will review progress.
markingPoints: Preparation: agenda, data and materials
Opening: aim, ground rules and parking lot
Idea generation that includes everyone, such as silent writing and round-robin
Narrowing and choosing: affinity grouping, multivoting, impact-effort, consensus
Close: target, owners, dates and review

essays.stem: In your team's improvement meetings, one member dominates the discussion and two members never speak. Explain how you would manage the group so that everyone contributes.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first think about why this happens. The dominant member may be keen and experienced, while the quiet members may lack confidence, be new or fear being judged. In the meeting, I would agree ground rules at the start, including one voice at a time and respect for every idea. I would use methods that give equal airtime, such as writing ideas silently on sticky notes before sharing, round-robin turns, and private voting with dots. I would invite quiet members by name with an easy, open question, and thank them when they speak. When the dominant member talks at length, I would politely summarise his point and say, "Let's hear from others now." I could also give him a useful role, such as recording ideas, which uses his energy without letting him control the discussion. Outside the meeting, I would speak to him privately to recognise his commitment and ask for his help in drawing others in. I would also speak with the quiet members one to one to understand any barriers and encourage them.
markingPoints: Considers the reasons behind each behaviour
Uses ground rules and structured techniques for equal input
Draws in quiet members supportively
Manages the dominant member respectfully in and out of the meeting
Keeps the group focused and positive

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can use coaching to build team members' ability to improve their own work. Illustrate your answer with the GROW model.
essays.modelAnswer: Coaching means helping a person find their own answers through questions, listening and support, rather than telling them what to do. It builds skill and confidence, so team members can spot and solve problems without waiting for the leader. The GROW model gives a simple structure. Take a clerk, Shanice, who makes frequent data entry errors. In the Goal stage, the leader asks what she wants to achieve, and they agree to cut her errors from ten a week to two within a month. In the Reality stage, the leader asks what is happening now: when the errors occur, and what gets in the way. Shanice notices that most errors happen when she is interrupted by phone calls. In the Options stage, the leader asks what she could do, and she suggests set times for answering calls, a checklist, or asking a colleague to check a sample. In the Way forward stage, she chooses an action, sets a date and agrees how progress will be checked. The leader follows up, gives feedback and praises progress, and later encourages Shanice to share what worked with the team.
markingPoints: Explains what coaching is and why it builds improvement skills
Goal: a clear, agreed target
Reality: exploring the current situation with questions
Options and Way forward: the person chooses actions and dates
Follow-up, feedback and sharing learning

essays.stem: Your team has introduced a better way of processing customer returns. Explain how you would make sure the improvement holds and becomes the normal way of working.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would write the new method down as standard work: a short, clear set of steps with photos or screen images, checked by the people who use it, and remove the old instructions so that nobody follows them by mistake. Every team member, including part-time and relief staff, would be trained in the new method and shown why it is better, and new staff would learn it during induction. I would add the method to any checklists and forms, and make sure the computer system and supplies support it. The team's measures for returns, such as the time to process and the error rate, would stay on the visual board, and we would review them at the weekly meeting for at least three months. If performance slips, we would find out why with the team, rather than blaming anyone, and fix the cause. I would recognise the team for keeping up the gain and tell other teams who deal with returns about the change. Finally, the standard is not fixed for ever: when someone finds a better way, we would test it and update the standard.
markingPoints: Documents the method as standard work and removes the old version
Trains all staff, including new and relief staff
Builds the method into forms, systems and checklists
Keeps measuring and reviews, acting on slippage without blame
Recognises the team and treats the standard as the base for further improvement

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader should communicate the team's improvement work to other teams, managers and customers, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Improvements in one team often affect others, so good communication avoids surprises and builds support. Other teams that send work to us or receive work from us should be consulted before a change that affects them, such as a new form or a new hand-over time, and told when it starts. This prevents errors and lets them suggest improvements too. Managers need short, regular updates, such as a monthly one-page report or a slide, showing the problem, the action, the results in figures and any help needed, like money or time. This keeps their support and lets them share good ideas across the organisation. Customers should be told about changes that affect them, such as new opening hours or a faster service, in plain language through the channels they use, and their feedback should be invited. Within the firm, success stories can be shared through staff newsletters, notice boards or meetings, giving credit to the team. Communicating well also recognises the team's effort, spreads good practice and shows that improvement is valued.
markingPoints: Consults affected teams before changes and informs them
Gives managers concise, evidence-based updates and requests
Informs customers clearly and seeks their feedback
Shares successes across the organisation with credit to the team
Explains why communication matters: support, fewer errors, spreading good practice

essays.stem: Evaluate a kaizen event compared with steady weekly improvement by a team, and recommend when a team leader should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: A kaizen event brings a small team together for a few focused days to study one process, design a better way and put it in place at once. Its strengths are speed and focus: a large change can be made in a week, the team sees results quickly, and people from different areas can work together. Its weaknesses are cost and disruption, because staff are taken away from their normal work, and gains may fade if there is no follow-up. Steady weekly improvement uses short huddles and weekly meetings in which the whole team makes many small changes over time. Its strengths are low cost, involvement of everyone and the habit of improving that it builds. Its weaknesses are that large or complex problems may move slowly and it can lose energy without good facilitation. I would recommend steady weekly improvement as the normal approach for every team. A kaizen event suits a clear, important problem in one process, such as a cluttered parcel sorting area causing delays, where a fast redesign is needed, with a plan to sustain the gains afterwards.
markingPoints: Describes a kaizen event with its strengths
Gives weaknesses of a kaizen event, such as cost or fading gains
Describes steady weekly improvement with strengths and weaknesses
Makes a fair comparison
Recommends when to use each, with an example

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can recognise contributions to continuous improvement fairly, and keep staff motivated without overloading them.
essays.modelAnswer: Recognition should be prompt, specific and fair. When someone suggests or tests an idea, the leader should thank them soon, say exactly what they did and show the result, for example at the weekly meeting or on the team board. Credit should go to everyone involved, including those who collected data or tried the new method, not only the person who had the idea, and the leader should never take the credit herself. Recognition should not depend only on money saved, because ideas that improve safety, customer service or teamwork also matter. Small rewards, such as a certificate or a mention in the staff newsletter, can be used if they follow clear rules applied to everyone. To avoid overload, the leader should plan improvement time into the roster, keep meetings short and focused, limit the number of actions running at once, and share tasks fairly so the same willing people are not always loaded. She should ask the team regularly how the workload feels, and pause or drop low-value actions. Staff stay motivated when they see that their ideas are used and their time is respected.
markingPoints: Recognition is prompt, specific and gives credit to all involved
Values non-financial gains as well as savings
Any rewards follow clear, fair rules
Plans time and limits work in progress to avoid overload
Checks workload with the team and shows ideas are acted on

practical1.title: Facilitate a team problem-solving session and agree an improvement action plan (role play)
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case card for a made-up team (for example the front desk of a Negril hotel, a supermarket checkout team in Portmore, or a claims team at an insurance office in Kingston) with four weeks of data on a problem such as long queues or errors. Your group runs a 45-minute improvement meeting as that team, which another group or the assessor observes, and produces the evidence. Give each member a named role: lead facilitator (opens the meeting, agrees ground rules, keeps time and the parking lot sheet), data analyst (turns the data into a run chart or bar chart on screen or flipchart and helps the group write a clear problem statement), idea facilitator (runs silent idea writing and a round-robin, then leads the group in an affinity diagram), decision facilitator (runs multivoting with dots and an impact-effort grid, and checks for consensus), and recorder (writes the SMART target and the action log with owners and dates). In a group of four, the lead facilitator also records. Members who are not leading a stage take part as team members. After the meeting, each member writes three lines on how well their stage went.
materials: Case card and four weeks of data from the assessor
Flipchart paper, sticky notes in two colours, sticky dots and markers
A computer with spreadsheet software, or graph paper
photos: The agenda and the ground rules on the flipchart
The chart of the data and the problem statement
The sticky-note ideas grouped into an affinity diagram
The multivoting dots and the impact-effort grid
The action log with SMART target, owners and dates
checklist: Took a named role and led their stage of the meeting
Kept to the agenda and the time for their stage
Used the technique for their stage correctly
Drew in all members and handled any off-topic points or disagreements calmly
The problem statement and SMART target are clear and based on the data
The action log has realistic actions with owners and dates
Reflected honestly on their own facilitation
safety: Use only the made-up team and data; do not discuss real colleagues or customers
Keep the role play respectful: challenge ideas, not people
Let any member step out of a role play that makes them uncomfortable
Take a short break between stages and keep a fair share of work

practical2.title: Build a team improvement board with standard work and a 30-day follow-up plan
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group an improvement that a made-up team has just agreed (for example a new way of processing customer returns at a hardware store in May Pen, or a new check-in routine at a guest house in Ocho Rios) and eight weeks of before-and-after data. As a group, prepare everything the team leader needs to make the change stick, and produce: a team improvement board on flipchart paper or a large poster, showing the team's measures, a run chart, an ideas column and the action status; the run chart built in a spreadsheet from the data, with the average before and after the change worked out and checked twice; a one-page standard work sheet for the new method; a 30-day follow-up plan with review dates, measures and a recognition plan; and a short email to the manager and other affected teams explaining the change and its results. Give each member a named role: board designer, data analyst (run chart and averages), standard work writer, trainer (uses the standard work sheet to train another member, playing a new staff member, in a short role play), and communicator (the email and recognition plan). In a group of four, the board designer also writes the recognition plan.
materials: Improvement card and eight weeks of data from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
Flipchart paper or poster board, markers, rulers and sticky notes
Printer or a way to show the work on screen
photos: The run chart on screen with the before and after averages
The trainer training the "new staff member" with the sheet
The email to the manager and other teams
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The run chart and averages are correct and clearly labelled
The board is clear enough for a team to read at a glance
The standard work sheet is accurate, in plain steps, and could be followed by a new person
The follow-up plan has dates, measures and fair recognition
The email is clear, brief and professional
